e1.bead.text: “For the road,” Naserian says. “Open your hand.” She offers you a bead to remember this meeting.

e1.bead.rest.beside.text: The women linger by the water. No one is in a hurry to say goodbye.

e1.carry.text: “Will you hold this while I speak?” Wambui asks.

e1.offer.beside.text: Wambui glances at the gourd beside you. “Help me set it here.” Touch the hide.

e1.offer.carried.text: “Set it here, beside me,” Wambui says. Touch the hide.

e1.paths.text: Imagine the paths that lead here: past millet fields and hives at the forest edge; out across the plain, where cattle graze. They meet at the water.

e1.touch.text: Put your hand in the water.

e1.water.felt.text: Your hand passes over the water. Enkare Nairobi. Cool water, in Maa, the Maasai language. A name the city will carry.

e1.water.heard.direction: Read the following passage aloud in the warm, unhurried cadence of a West African griot — resonant, deep, with occasional pauses for emphasis. Let the words breathe. This is oral storytelling, not news reading.
e1.water.heard.text: The stream runs beside you. Enkare Nairobi. Cool water, in Maa, the Maasai language. A name the city will carry.

q.e1.bead.answer.direction: Read the following passage aloud in the warm, unhurried cadence of a West African griot — resonant, deep, with occasional pauses for emphasis. Let the words breathe. This is oral storytelling, not news reading.
q.e1.bead.answer.text: A way to remember an afternoon by the water. This gift is our invention; its colour carries no traditional meaning in this telling.

q.e1.flour.answer.direction: Read the following passage aloud in the warm, unhurried cadence of a West African griot — resonant, deep, with occasional pauses for emphasis. Let the words breathe. This is oral storytelling, not news reading.
q.e1.flour.answer.text: Green bananas, dried and pounded. There are accounts of this flour being traded for sheep. How much Wambui owes today belongs to our story.

q.e1.friends.answer.direction: Read the following passage aloud in the warm, unhurried cadence of a West African griot — resonant, deep, with occasional pauses for emphasis. Let the words breathe. This is oral storytelling, not news reading.
q.e1.friends.answer.text: They have met here before. Each has had to wait for the other. That friendship is ours to imagine; trade and marriage really did join their communities.

q.e1.milk.answer.direction: Read the following passage aloud in the warm, unhurried cadence of a West African griot — resonant, deep, with occasional pauses for emphasis. Let the words breathe. This is oral storytelling, not news reading.
q.e1.milk.answer.text: Milk. A museum in Nairobi keeps a Maasai gourd smoked inside with oloirien wood. Imagine that trace of smoke in the vessel Naserian has brought.

q.e1.trust.answer.direction: Read the following passage aloud in the warm, unhurried cadence of a West African griot — resonant, deep, with occasional pauses for emphasis. Let the words breathe. This is oral storytelling, not news reading.
q.e1.trust.answer.text: Naserian remembers needing time herself. Wambui waited then. Now it is her turn. The sheep matters; so does seeing Wambui come back.

q.today.who.answer.direction: Read the following passage aloud in the warm, unhurried cadence of a West African griot — resonant, deep, with occasional pauses for emphasis. Let the words breathe. This is oral storytelling, not news reading.
q.today.who.answer.text: In our imagined garden, neighbours planted it together. Someone brought seedlings; someone carried water. Tomorrow, someone must come back to tend it.

today.bead.ask.text: There is a place on the gate for the bead. Touch the gate to leave it here, for someone else to find.

today.rubbish.text: Along this river, neighbours have cleared rubbish and planted places to gather and grow. The work is unfinished. This little garden is imagined; the work that inspired it is real.

welcome.choose.text: Reach out when you are ready. A fire is patient.
